wade.e: From Middle English waden, from Old English wadan, from Proto-West Germanic *wadan, from Proto-Germanic *wadaną (“to go, pass through”), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₂dʰ- (“to go”).
wade.g: To walk through water or something that impedes progress.

wadi.e: Borrowed from Arabic وَادِي, وَادٍ (wādī, wādin, “valley, riverbed, ravine”).
wadi.g: A valley, gully, or stream bed in northern Africa and southwest Asia that remains dry except during the rainy season.

wafer.e: From Middle English wafre, from Anglo-Norman wafre, waufre (Old French gaufre), from a Germanic source.

wag.e: From Middle English waggen, probably from Old English wagian (“to wag, wave, shake”) with reinforcement from Old Norse vaga (“to wag, waddle”); both from Proto-Germanic *wagōną (“to wag”). The verb may be regarded as an iterative or emphatic form of waw (verb), which is often nearly synonymous; it was used, e.g., of a loose tooth.
wag.g: To swing from side to side, as an animal's tail, or someone's head to express disagreement or disbelief.

wage.e: From Middle English wage, from Anglo-Norman wage, from Old Northern French wage, a northern variant of Old French gauge, guage (whence modern French gage), Medieval Latin wadium, from Frankish *waddī (cognate with Old English wedd), from Proto-Germanic *wadją (“pledge”), from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ- (“to pledge, redeem a pledge”).
wage.g: An amount of money paid to a worker for a specified quantity of work, usually calculated on an hourly basis and expressed in an amount of mo

wage.e: From Middle English wagen (“to pledge”), from Anglo-Norman, Old Northern French wagier, a northern variant of Old French guagier (whence modern French gager), itself either from guage or from a derivative of Frankish *waddī, possibly through a Vulgar Latin intermediate *wadiō from *wadium (see the noun above).

wagon.e: Borrowed from Middle Dutch wagen, from Old Dutch *wagan, from Proto-West Germanic *wagn, from Proto-Germanic *wagnaz (“wagon”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to transport”). Generally displaced native cognate wain, from Old English wæġn, of which it is a doublet. Related also to way, weigh. Sense 8 (“woman of loose morals.
wagon.g: A heavier four-wheeled (normally horse-drawn) vehicle designed to carry goods (or sometimes people).

wail.e: c. 1300, Middle English weilen, waylen (“to sob, cry, wail”), from Old Norse væla (“to wail”), from væ, vei (“woe”), from Proto-Germanic *wai (whence also Old English wā (“woe”) (English woe)), from Proto-Indo-European *wáy. The noun came from the verb.
wail.g: To cry out, as in sorrow or anguish.
Synonym of wale (“to choose; to select”).

waist.e: From Middle English wast (“waist”), probably from Old English *wæst, *wǣst, *weaxt, *wæhst, from Proto-West Germanic *wahstu, from Proto-Germanic *wahstuz (“growth, development, stature, build”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weks- (“to multiply, increase”).
waist.g: The part of the body between the pelvis and the stomach.

waistband.g: A band of fabric encircling the waist, especially a part of a pair of pants or a skirt.

wait.e: From Middle English waiten, from Anglo-Norman waiter, waitier (compare French guetter from Old French gaitier, guaitier), from Frankish *wahtwēn (“to watch, guard”), derivative of Frankish *wahtu (“guard, watch”), from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō (“guard, watch”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵ- (“to be fresh, cheerful, awake”).
wait.g: To delay movement or action until some event or time; to remain neglected or in readiness.
The last tile a player requires to complete a winning hand

waiting.e: From Middle English waitinge, waytynge, waitende, weytende, waitand, waytand, equivalent to wait + -ing.

wake.e: A merger of two verbs of related/similar form and meaning: Middle English waken, Old English wacan, from Proto-West Germanic *wakan, from Proto-Germanic *wakaną. Middle English wakien, Old English wacian, from Proto-West Germanic *wakēn, from Proto-Germanic *wakāną.
wake.g: (often followed by up) To stop sleeping.

wake.e: From Middle English wake, from Old English wacu, from Proto-Germanic *wakō, related to the verb *wakjaną.
wake.g: A period after a person's death before or after the body is buried, cremated, etc.; in some cultures accompanied by a party or collectively

waken.e: From Middle English waknen, from Old English wæcnan, from Proto-Germanic *waknaną.
waken.g: To wake or rouse from sleep.

walk.e: From Middle English walk, walke, walken, walkyn, wolken (“to roll, toss, or turn; to walk; to move; to be living; to beat or full; to perform”), a conflation of Old English wealcan (“to move around; to revolve; to roll; to fluctuate; to discuss”) (ġewealcan (“to go, traverse; to roll”)) and Old English wealcian (“to curl, roll up, twist; to wrinkle”).
walk.g: To move on the feet by alternately setting each foot (or pair or group of feet: in the case of some non-human animals with four or more feet

walk.e: From Middle English walc, walk, walke, from Old English *wealc (as in Old English wealcspinl) and ġewealc (“rolling, turning; motion, surging”), from Proto-Germanic *walką.

walking.e: From Middle English walkynge, walkinge, walkinde, walkende, walkand, walkande, from Old English wealcende (attested as Old English wealcendes), from Proto-Germanic *walkandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *walkaną (“to roll, trample, walk”), equivalent to walk + -ing.

wall.e: From Middle English wal, from Old English weall (“wall, dike, earthwork, rampart, dam, rocky shore, cliff”), from Proto-West Germanic *wall (“wall, rampart, entrenchment”), from Latin vallum (“wall, rampart, entrenchment, palisade”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn, wind, roll”).
wall.g: A rampart of earth, stones etc. built up for defensive purposes.

wall.e: From Middle English wallen, from Old English weallan (“to bubble, boil”), from Proto-West Germanic *wallan, from Proto-Germanic *wallaną (“to fount, stream, boil”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“wave”).

wallow.e: From Middle English walowen, walewen, walwen, welwen, from Old English wealwian (“to roll”), from Proto-West Germanic *walwōn, variant of *walwijan, from Proto-Germanic *walwijaną (“to roll”), from Proto-Indo-European *welw-, from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn, wind, roll”).
wallow.g: To roll oneself about in something dirty, for example in mud.

wallow.e: From Middle English walwen, from Old English wealwian (“to fade, wither”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps an alteration of Old English fealwian (“to grow pale, turn yellow, ripen, wither”). Alternatively, perhaps related to Middle English welken (“to fade, droop, wither”), modern English welk.
wallow.g: To fade, fade away, wither, droop; fail to flourish.

walnut.e: From Middle English walnote, walnutte, walnotte, from Old English wealhhnutu (“walnut”, literally “foreign nut”), from Proto-Germanic *walhahnuts (literally “foreigner-nut”).
walnut.g: A hardwood tree of the genus Juglans.

wander.e: From Middle English wandren, from Old English wandrian (“to wander, roam, fly around, hover; change; stray, err”), from Proto-West Germanic *wandarōn (“to wander”), from *wandōn (“to turn, change”) + *-rōn (frequentative suffix).
wander.g: To move without purpose or specified destination; often in search of livelihood.

wanderer.e: From Middle English wanderere, wandrere, wanderare, equivalent to wander + -er.
wanderer.g: One who wanders, who travels aimlessly.

wandering.g: Which wanders; travelling from place to place.

wane.e: From Middle English wane, from Old English wana (“defect, shortage”), from Proto-West Germanic *wanō, from Proto-Germanic *wanô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“to leave, abandon; empty, deserted”).
wane.g: A gradual diminution in power, value, intensity etc.

wane.e: From Middle English wanen, wanien, from Old English wanian, wonian, from Proto-West Germanic *wanōn, from Proto-Germanic *wanōną.
wane.g: To progressively lose its splendor, value, ardor, power, intensity etc.; to decline.

want.e: From Middle English wanten (“to lack, to need”), from Old Norse vanta (“to lack”), from Proto-Germanic *wanatōną (“to be wanting, lack”), from *wanô (“lack, deficiency”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“empty”).
want.g: To wish for or desire (something); to feel a need or desire for; to crave, hanker, or demand.

want.e: From Middle English wont (“mole”), from Old English wand, wond, from Proto-Germanic *wanduz.

wanting.e: From Middle English wantyng, wantynge, wantand, equivalent to want + -ing.

wanton.e: From Middle English wantoun, wantowen, wantoȝen, wantowe (“uneducated; unrestrained; licentious; sportive; playful”), from wan- (“not, un-, mis-”) + towen, i-towen (“educated”, literally “towed; led; drawn”), from Old English togen, ġetogen, past participle of tēon (“to train, discipline”), equivalent to wan- + towed.
wanton.g: Undisciplined, unruly; not able to be controlled.

wanton.e: Borrowed from Cantonese 雲吞 /云吞 (wan⁴ tan¹).

wantonness.e: From Middle English wantonnesse, wantonesse, wantounesse, wantownesse, equivalent to wanton + -ness.
wantonness.g: The state or characteristic of being wanton; recklessness, especially as represented in lascivious or other excessive behavior.

war.e: From Middle English werre, from Late Old English werre /wyrre (“armed conflict”), from Anglo-Norman and Old Northern French guerre /werre (compare modern French guerre), from Medieval Latin werra, from Frankish *werʀu (“confusion; quarrel”), from Proto-Indo-European *wers- (“to mix up, confuse, beat, thresh”).
war.g: Organized, large-scale, armed conflict between countries or between national, ethnic, or other sizeable groups, usually but not always invol

ward.e: From Middle English warde, from Old English weard (“keeper, watchman, guard, guardian, protector; lord, king; possessor”), from Proto-Germanic *warduz (“guard, keeper”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to heed, defend”).
ward.g: A warden; a guard; a guardian or watchman.

ward.e: From Middle English ward, warde, from Old English weard (“watching, ward, protection, guardianship; advance post; waiting for, lurking, ambuscade”), from Proto-West Germanic *wardu, from Proto-Germanic *wardō (“protection, attention, keeping”), an extension of the stem *wara- (“attentive”) (English wary, beware), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to cover”).

warden.e: From Middle English wardein, from Anglo-Norman wardein, from warder (“to guard”), variant of Old French guarder (“to guard”) (whence modern French garder, also English guard), from Proto-Germanic *wardāną; related to Old High German wartēn (“to watch”).
From Middle English wardon, origin uncertain; perhaps from Anglo-Norman or Anglo-Latin wardo, -ōnis.

wardrobe.e: From Middle English warderobe, from Old Northern French warderoube, wardereube, northern variants of Old French garderobe, from garder (“to keep safe”) + robe. Subsequently influenced by various senses of garderobe as they developed in French. By surface analysis, ward + robe.
wardrobe.g: A room for keeping clothes and armor safe, particularly a dressing room or walk-in closet beside a bedroom.

ware.e: From Middle English ware, from Old English waru, from Proto-West Germanic *waru, from Proto-Germanic *warō (“attention”) as in beware, in the sense of “an object of care, a valuable”, from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to watch, keep guard”), whence also ward.
ware.g: Goods or a type of goods offered for sale or use.

ware.e: From Middle English waren (“to be ware, be on guard, be mindful, protect, guard”), from Old English warian, from Proto-West Germanic *warōn, from Proto-Germanic *warōną.
ware.g: To be ware or mindful of something.

warfare.e: From war + fare; perhaps a shortening of Middle English werre-faringe, werfarynge (“waging war, warfare”, literally “going to war”).
warfare.g: The waging of war or armed conflict against an enemy.

warm.e: From Middle English warm, werm, from Old English wearm, from Proto-West Germanic *warm, from Proto-Germanic *warmaz, from one of: Proto-Indo-European *wór-mo-s, from *wer- (“to burn”), which is related to Hittite 𒉿𒊏𒀀𒉌 (warāni, “to burn”), Armenian վառել (vaṙel, “to burn, heat, warm”), Old Church Slavonic варити (variti, “to cook, boil”).
warm.g: Of a somewhat high temperature, often but not always connoting that the high temperature is pleasant rather than uncomfortable.

warm.e: From Middle English warmen, wermen, wyrmen, from Old English wierman (“to make warm”) and wearmian (“to become warm”), from Proto-West Germanic *warmijan and *warmōn.

warming.e: From Middle English warminge, warmynge, from Old English wærmiġende, wermende, wyrmende, present participle of Old English wyrman, wirman (“to warm”), equivalent to warm + -ing.
warming.g: Having a warm quality; causing warmth or a warm feeling, such as coziness, comfort, affection, etc.

warmth.e: From Middle English warmth, warmeth, wermþe, from Old English *wiermþu (“warmth”), from Proto-West Germanic *warmiþu (“warmness; warmth”), corresponding to warm + -th (abstract nominal suffix).
warmth.g: A moderate degree of heat; the sensation of being warm.

warn.e: From Middle English warnen, warnien (“to warn; admonish”), from Old English warnian (“to take heed; warn”), from Proto-Germanic *warnōną (“to warn; take heed”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to be aware; give heed”).
warn.g: To make (someone) aware of (something impending); especially:

warp.e: From Middle English warp, werp, from Old English wearp, warp (“a warp, threads stretched lengthwise in a loom, twig, osier”), from Proto-Germanic *warpą (“a warp”).
warp.g: The state, quality, or condition of being twisted, physically or mentally:

warp.e: From Middle English werpen, weorpen, worpen, from Old English weorpan (“to throw”), from Proto-West Germanic *werpan, from Proto-Germanic *werpaną (“to throw, turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *werb- (“to bend, turn”).
warp.g: To twist or become twisted, physically or mentally.

warrant.e: The word is cognate with Old High German werento (“guarantor”).
warrant.g: Authorization or certification; a sanction, as given by a superior.

warring.e: From Middle English werrynge. By surface analysis, war + -ing.

warrior.e: From Middle English werreour, from Anglo-Norman werreur, Old French guerroiier (“fighter, combattant”), from Medieval Latin werra, from Frankish *werʀu (“confusion; quarrel”), from Proto-Indo-European *wers- (“to mix up, confuse, beat, thresh”).
warrior.g: A person who is actively engaged in battle, conflict or warfare; a soldier or combatant.

wash.e: From Middle English wasshen, waschen (“to wash”), from Old English wascan (“to wash”), from Proto-West Germanic *waskan (“to wash”), from Proto-Germanic *waskaną, *watskaną (“to wash, get wet”), from Proto-Indo-European *wed- (“wet, water”).

washbasin.g: A basin used for washing, (now) particularly a permanently installed sink, fitted with a water supply and a drain, for washing the hands and

washing.e: From Middle English waschynge /wasshynge, from Old English *wæsċende /*wasċende, from Proto-West Germanic *waskandī, from Proto-Germanic *waskandz (“washing”), present participle of *waskaną (“to wash”). By surface analysis, wash + -ing.

washpot.g: A pot which holds water for washing.

wasn't.e: Contraction of was + not. By surface analysis, was + -n't.

waste.e: From Middle English wast, waste (“a waste”, noun), from Anglo-Norman, Old Northern French wast, waste (“a waste”), from Frankish *wōstī (“a waste”), from Proto-Germanic *wōstaz, *wōstuz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“empty, wasted”).
waste.g: Excess of material, useless by-products, or damaged, unsaleable products; garbage; rubbish.

waste.e: From Middle English wast, waste (“waste”, adjective), from Anglo-Norman, Old Northern French wast (“waste”), from Frankish *wōstī (“waste, empty”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“empty, wasted”).

wasteland.e: From Middle English wast lond, modification of earlier weste lond, from Old English weste land (“wasteland”); equivalent to waste + land.
wasteland.g: A place with no remaining resources; a desert.

wasteness.e: From Middle English wastnesse; equivalent to waste + -ness.
wasteness.g: The state of being laid waste; desolation.

waster.e: From Middle English wastere, waister, wastar, wastour, equivalent to waste + -er.
waster.g: Someone or something that wastes; someone who squanders or spends extravagantly.

watch.e: As a noun, from Middle English wacche, from Old English wæċċe.
From Middle English wacchen, from Old English wæċċan, from Proto-West Germanic *wakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *wakjaną.
watch.g: To look at, see, or view for a period of time.

watched.e: From watch (“a portable or wearable timepiece”) + -ed (“having”).
watched.g: Wearing a watch (a portable or wearable timepiece).

watcher.e: From Middle English wacchere, wachere, wacher, equivalent to watch + -er.

watchful.e: From Middle English waccheful, equivalent to watch + -ful.

watchman.e: From Middle English waccheman. By surface analysis, watch + -man.
watchman.g: A man set to watch: a man who keeps guard, especially one who guards a building, or the streets of a city, by night; (loosely) any such pers

water.e: From Middle English water, from Old English wæter (“water”), from Proto-West Germanic *watar, from Proto-Germanic *watōr (“water”), from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ (“water”).
water.g: An inorganic compound (of molecular formula H₂O) found at room temperature and pressure as a clear liquid; it is present naturally as rain,

water.e: From Middle English wateren, from Old English wæterian, from Proto-Germanic *watrōną, *watrijaną, from Proto-Germanic *watōr (“water”), from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ (“water”).
water.g: To wet or supply with water; to moisten; to overflow with water; to irrigate.

watercourse.e: From Middle English water course; equivalent to water + course.
watercourse.g: Any channel, either natural or artificial, through which water flows.

watered.e: From Middle English watered, watred, ywaterd, y-wattered, i-watred, i-watered, from Old English *wæterod, *ġewæterod, equivalent to water + -ed.

waterfall.e: From Middle English waterfal, waterfalle, from Old English wæterġefeall (“waterfall”), equivalent to water + fall.
waterfall.g: A flow of water over the edge of a cliff.

waterflood.e: From Middle English waterrflod, from Old English wæterflōd, equivalent to water + flood.

waterless.e: From Middle English waterles, waterlees, from Old English wæterlēas (“waterless”), from Proto-Germanic *watōrlausaz, equivalent to water + -less.

waterpot.e: From Middle English waterpot, waterpott, water pott, watyrpotte, equivalent to water + pot.
waterpot.g: A pot or jug for holding water.

waterspout.g: A whirlwind that forms over water, not associated with a mesocyclone of a thunderstorm (contrary to a true tornado).

waterway.e: From Middle English waterwey, from Old English wæterweġ (“waterway”), from Proto-West Germanic *watarweg, equivalent to water + way.
waterway.g: A body of water, such as a river, channel or canal, that is navigable.

watery.e: From Middle English watery, wattry, from Old English wæteriġ (“watery”), from Proto-West Germanic *watarīg. Equivalent to water + -y.

wave.e: From Middle English waven, from Old English wafian (“to wave, fluctuate, waver in mind, wonder”), from Proto-West Germanic *wabōn, from Proto-Germanic *wabōną, *wabjaną (“to wander, sway”), from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to move to and from, wander”).
wave.g: To move back and forth repeatedly and somewhat loosely.

wave.e: From Middle English *wave, partially from waven (“to fluctuate, wave”) (see above) and partially from Middle English wawe, waghe (“wave”), from Old English wǣg (“a wave, billow, motion, water, flood, sea”), from Proto-Germanic *wēgaz (“motion, storm, wave”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to drag, carry”).
wave.g: A moving disturbance in the level of a body of liquid; an undulation.

waver.g: One who waves their arms, or causes something to swing or wave.

waver.e: Origin uncertain, possibly from waive (“(obsolete) to disregard, overlook”). According to the Oxford English Dictionary the early forms waiver, wayver, weaver indicate that the word is probably not derived from wave (verb).
waver.g: A sapling or other young tree left standing when other trees around it have been felled.

wax.e: From Middle English wax, from Old English weax, from Proto-Germanic *wahsą, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *woḱ-so-.
wax.g: Any oily, water-resistant, solid or semisolid substance; normally long-chain hydrocarbons, alcohols or esters.

wax.e: From Middle English waxen, from the noun (see above).
wax.g: To apply wax to (something, such as a shoe, a floor, a car, or an apple), usually to make it shiny.

waxen.e: From Middle English waxen, from Old English weaxen, ġeweaxen, from Proto-Germanic *wahsanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *wahsijaną (“to wax, grow, increase”), equivalent to wax + -en (past participle ending).

way.e: From Middle English way, wey, from Old English weġ, from Proto-West Germanic *weg, from Proto-Germanic *wegaz, from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-.
way.g: To do with a place or places.

wayfaring.e: From Middle English wayferande, weyverinde, wayverinde, from Old English weġfarende, weġfērende (“wayfaring”), equivalent to way + faring.

waymark.g: A sign or symbol marked in a prominent position in an off-road location to show the track of a footpath or route; fingerpost; guidepost; mil

wayside.e: From Middle English waye syde, equivalent to way + side.
wayside.g: The side of a road or path.

wayward.g: Given to a wilful, perverse deviation from the expected norm; tending to stray.

be.e: From Middle English been (“to be”). Further etymology of be and its conjugated forms The various forms have three separate origins, which were mixed together at various times in the history of English. The forms beginning with b- come from Old English bēon (“to be, become”), from Proto-Germanic *beuną (“to be, exist, come to be, become”).
A variant of by which goes back to Middle English be (variant of Middle English bi).
be.g: Alternative form of by. Also found in compounds, especially oaths, e.g. begorra begad and bejesus.
